snapshots.name: René Descartes
snapshots.body: The philosopher, praised in the Preface for having doubted honestly and for confining his method's claims to himself -- unlike, in Johannes de Silentio's telling, the philosophers of the present age.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Johannes de Silentio
snapshots.body: The pseudonym under which this book is written and signed; "the present author" who speaks throughout in the first person.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Abraham
snapshots.body: The patriarch whose willingness to sacrifice Isaac at God's command is this book's subject throughout: the "father of faith" whom Johannes de Silentio admires but cannot understand.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Isaac
snapshots.body: Abraham's son, born to Sarah in her old age against expectation, and the one Abraham is commanded to sacrifice on Mount Moriah.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Sarah
snapshots.body: Abraham's wife, who bore Isaac in her old age; in Problema III, one of the three -- with Eliezer and Isaac -- from whom Abraham conceals his undertaking.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Sarah (Book of Tobit)
snapshots.body: A different Sarah: the daughter of Raguel and Edna in the Book of Tobit, given to seven husbands who each died on the wedding night before Tobias married her and survived. Kierkegaard calls her a heroine.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hagar
snapshots.body: Abraham's concubine, mother of his son Ishmael, whom Abraham drove out into the wilderness -- recalled in the Exordium's third retelling and again in Problema II.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eliezer
snapshots.body: Abraham's faithful servant, named in the Exordium and again in Problema III as one of the three from whom Abraham conceals his undertaking on the way to Moriah.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Moses
snapshots.body: Recalled for having struck the rock with his staff without believing, contrasted with Abraham and Sarah's belief in the promise.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jacob
snapshots.body: Abraham's grandson, recalled as having had twelve sons and yet loving one -- Joseph -- as Abraham loved his only Isaac.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Noureddin
snapshots.body: A caliph of the Arabian Nights, invoked alongside Aladdin as an example of one who merely holds a magic ring of power, indifferent to how he came by it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aladdin
snapshots.body: The Arabian Nights hero, invoked alongside Noureddin as an example of one who merely holds a magic ring of power, indifferent to how he came by it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Orpheus
snapshots.body: The legendary musician, recalled as having been deceived by the gods with an airy phantom in place of his beloved -- Johannes de Silentio's image for getting nothing without working.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Miltiades
snapshots.body: The Athenian general at Marathon, whose famous triumphs, Johannes de Silentio notes, thousands knew by heart while only one man -- Themistocles, though unnamed here -- lost sleep over them.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jesus Christ
snapshots.body: Recalled as the one the rich young man met on his way, and later as the one it would be sweet to imagine walking the promised land -- forgetting how dreadful it actually was to have sat at table with God.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: G. W. F. Hegel
snapshots.body: The philosopher whose account of the single individual, the ethical, and inwardness Johannes de Silentio repeatedly takes up and disputes, faulting him above all for speaking of Abraham as a father of faith.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Esau
snapshots.body: Jacob's brother, recalled only for the strength of his appetite, to which the knight of infinite resignation's wife-imagined roast lamb dinner is compared.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Karl Daub
snapshots.body: The German theologian, quoted on the strange thoughts of a lone sentry standing watch by a powder magazine on a stormy night.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Herod
snapshots.body: Named alongside Pilate as a figure a young maiden's naive religious assurance might run to and sway with her prayers.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pontius Pilate
snapshots.body: Named alongside Herod as a figure a young maiden's naive religious assurance might run to and sway with her prayers.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Nicolas Boileau
snapshots.body: The French critic, quoted on how a fool always finds a bigger fool to admire him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Agamemnon
snapshots.body: The Greek commander at Aulis, who must sacrifice his daughter Iphigenia to obtain a favorable wind for the fleet -- Johannes de Silentio's recurring tragic-hero counterpart to Abraham.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Iphigenia
snapshots.body: Agamemnon's daughter, sacrificed (in Euripides's play) to secure the fleet's passage to Troy -- the tragic-hero's counterpart to Isaac, who unlike Isaac is told, weeps, and understands.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jephthah
snapshots.body: The judge of Israel who, bound by his own vow, sacrifices his daughter after she is granted two months to mourn her lost youth -- another of the tragic-hero counterparts to Abraham.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lucius Junius Brutus
snapshots.body: The Roman consul who, entrusted with judgment as a father, is said to have ordered the execution of his own son for treason against the young republic -- a third tragic-hero counterpart to Abraham.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: William Shakespeare
snapshots.body: Addressed directly ("great Shakespeare") as the poet who could say anything, wondered at for never having given voice to Abraham's particular anguish -- and named again as the author of Richard III.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pythagoras
snapshots.body: The Greek philosopher, cited for the saying that the odd number is more perfect than the even, and later for having chosen death over breaking his habitual silence.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Judas Iscariot
snapshots.body: Recalled as having sold his Lord for thirty pieces of silver -- the standard of contempt Johannes de Silentio measures against one who cheapens the story of Abraham by dwelling only on its outcome.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Virgin Mary
snapshots.body: Mother of Jesus, held up as another figure made great not by favor alone but by the distress, anguish, and paradox that favor brought her.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
snapshots.body: Cited for a kind of misdirected love -- loving distant Kaffirs in place of one's actual neighbor -- that Johannes de Silentio compares to loving an abstracted "God."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Socrates
snapshots.body: The Athenian philosopher, called the most interesting man who ever lived; his ironic reply to his own death sentence is discussed at length as the model of a fitting last word for an intellectual tragic hero.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cain
snapshots.body: The first murderer, invoked to distinguish Abraham from him: Abraham does not hate Isaac as Cain hated Abel, which is precisely what makes Abraham's willingness a sacrifice rather than a murder.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Master Jakel
snapshots.body: A stock puppet-theatre showman figure (comparable to Punch), invoked as a type for the sectarian who gathers a few admiring friends and mistakes them for the universal.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aristotle
snapshots.body: The philosopher, cited from the Poetics on recognition and reversal in tragedy, and from the Politics for the story of the bridegroom of Delphi used later in the same chapter.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Euripides
snapshots.body: The Greek tragedian, whose Iphigenia in Aulis supplies the Agamemnon example Johannes de Silentio analyzes at length.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Clytemnestra
snapshots.body: Agamemnon's wife and Iphigenia's mother, whose tears (and an old servant's disclosure to her) are part of the aesthetic apparatus of the Iphigenia story.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Amor (Cupid)
snapshots.body: The god of love in the myth of Cupid and Psyche, who leaves Psyche with the warning that her child will be divine only if she keeps his identity secret.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Psyche
snapshots.body: Amor's beloved in the myth, warned that betraying his secret will cost her child its divinity -- Johannes de Silentio's image for how silence itself can be great.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing
snapshots.body: The German critic and dramatist, thanked for his brief remarks on a possible Christian drama in the Hamburg Dramaturgy, and praised for never claiming to have understood more than he had.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Queen Elizabeth I
snapshots.body: The English queen, who signed the Earl of Essex's death warrant for the sake of the state -- and who, on learning too late that he had in fact sent her the ring she'd waited for, is said to have died in silence.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex
snapshots.body: Elizabeth I's favorite, whose death warrant she signed; his ring, sent to beg her mercy, was withheld from her by a lady-in-waiting's malice.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Axel
snapshots.body: One half of the title pair of Oehlenschläger's tragedy Axel and Valborg, invoked as an example of lovers whom heaven itself separates equally, unlike the bridegroom of Delphi.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Valborg
snapshots.body: The other half of the title pair of Oehlenschläger's tragedy Axel and Valborg, invoked as an example of lovers whom heaven itself separates equally, unlike the bridegroom of Delphi.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Laban
snapshots.body: Jacob's father-in-law in Genesis, invoked as a type for the man in poetry who abandons one woman for her more "ideal" sister and thereby confuses trivial substitution for real passionate collision.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Agnete (Agnes)
snapshots.body: The innocent girl of the Danish legend of Agnete and the Merman, whose steady, believing gaze -- in Johannes de Silentio's retelling -- disarms the Merman's power to seduce her.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Merman
snapshots.body: The seducer of the legend of Agnete and the Merman; Johannes de Silentio reworks the story twice, once as a demonic figure conquered by Agnete's innocence, once as a genuinely repentant figure who might be saved by her love.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Gloster (Richard III)
snapshots.body: Shakespeare's Richard, Duke of Gloucester and later Richard III, called the most demonic figure Shakespeare ever portrayed, made a demon by an inability to bear the compassion shown him from childhood for his deformity.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Richard Cumberland
snapshots.body: The English playwright; "Cumberland's Jew" refers to Sheva, the sympathetic Jewish character of Cumberland's 1794 play The Jew, cited here as another demonic figure despite doing what is good.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jens Baggesen
snapshots.body: The Danish poet, quoted on the immortality of a mediocre city poet named Kildevalle: "if he becometh immortal, then become we all so."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Faust
snapshots.body: The doubter of German legend; Johannes de Silentio proposes his own version, one who loves Margaret but stays silent about his doubt out of sympathy for mankind, sacrificing himself for the universal.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
snapshots.body: The poet, whose interpretation of Faust Johannes de Silentio finds lacking in psychological insight into doubt's own inner conversations.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mephistopheles
snapshots.body: The demon of Goethe's Faust, whose "concave mirror" is contrasted with the clear, innocent way Johannes de Silentio's own imagined Faust sees Margaret.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Margaret (Gretchen)
snapshots.body: Faust's beloved in Goethe's drama, seen here in her full innocence rather than through Mephistopheles's distorting mirror.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aristophanes
snapshots.body: The Greek comic playwright, imagined as the one who might, on purely ethical grounds, let laughter pass judgment on a bewildered age.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Baron Munchausen
snapshots.body: The legendary teller of tall tales, invoked as the contrast to a man who has genuinely undergone spiritual trial: one can tell the difference by listening through the line of what is said.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tamerlane
snapshots.body: The conqueror, whose power to terrify with his armies is compared to what Faust's doubt could do to men's security, if he chose to speak it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Gregory of Rimini
snapshots.body: The medieval theologian nicknamed "tortor infantium" ("torturer of infants") for holding that unbaptized children are damned -- a nickname Johannes de Silentio borrows, calling himself "tortor heroum," a torturer of heroes.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tobias
snapshots.body: The young man of the Book of Tobit who marries Sarah, knowing the demon that killed her seven previous husbands on their wedding nights, and survives.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Raguel
snapshots.body: Sarah's father in the Book of Tobit, who has a grave dug in the night in case Tobias too should die, and asks a maid to check whether he lives.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Edna
snapshots.body: Sarah's mother in the Book of Tobit, who prepares the bridal chamber, weeps with her daughter, and blesses her before the wedding night.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Longus
snapshots.body: The Greek author of the pastoral romance Daphnis and Chloe, cited (as "Longi Pastoralia") for the line that no one has ever escaped Love, nor will, so long as beauty exists and eyes can see.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Achilles
snapshots.body: Named among those present at Aulis -- with Clytemnestra, Iphigenia, and the chorus -- whose grief and argument the tragic hero Agamemnon must, and does, face and answer.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Edward IV
snapshots.body: The English king, quoted (in German) lamenting, on hearing of his brother Clarence's murder, that no one had pleaded for him -- the outcry Abraham is spared, since no one else can even argue with him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: George, Duke of Clarence
snapshots.body: Edward IV's brother, whose murder -- from Shakespeare's Richard III -- prompts the king's lament that no one had pleaded on his behalf.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Calchas

snapshots.name: Judas Iscariot
snapshots.body: Recalled as having sold his Lord for thirty pieces of silver -- the standard of contempt Johannes de Silentio measures against one who cheapens the story of Abraham by dwelling only on its outcome.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Virgin Mary
snapshots.body: Mother of Jesus, held up as another figure made great not by favor alone but by the distress, anguish, and paradox that favor brought her.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
snapshots.body: Cited for a kind of misdirected love -- loving distant Kaffirs in place of one's actual neighbor -- that Johannes de Silentio compares to loving an abstracted "God."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Socrates
snapshots.body: The Athenian philosopher, called the most interesting man who ever lived; his ironic reply to his own death sentence is discussed at length as the model of a fitting last word for an intellectual tragic hero.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cain
snapshots.body: The first murderer, invoked to distinguish Abraham from him: Abraham does not hate Isaac as Cain hated Abel, which is precisely what makes Abraham's willingness a sacrifice rather than a murder.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Master Jakel
snapshots.body: A stock puppet-theatre showman figure (comparable to Punch), invoked as a type for the sectarian who gathers a few admiring friends and mistakes them for the universal.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aristotle
snapshots.body: The philosopher, cited from the Poetics on recognition and reversal in tragedy, and from the Politics for the story of the bridegroom of Delphi used later in the same chapter.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Euripides
snapshots.body: The Greek tragedian, whose Iphigenia in Aulis supplies the Agamemnon example Johannes de Silentio analyzes at length.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Clytemnestra
snapshots.body: Agamemnon's wife and Iphigenia's mother, whose tears (and an old servant's disclosure to her) are part of the aesthetic apparatus of the Iphigenia story.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Amor (Cupid)
snapshots.body: The god of love in the myth of Cupid and Psyche, who leaves Psyche with the warning that her child will be divine only if she keeps his identity secret.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Psyche
snapshots.body: Amor's beloved in the myth, warned that betraying his secret will cost her child its divinity -- Johannes de Silentio's image for how silence itself can be great.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing
snapshots.body: The German critic and dramatist, thanked for his brief remarks on a possible Christian drama in the Hamburg Dramaturgy, and praised for never claiming to have understood more than he had.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Queen Elizabeth I
snapshots.body: The English queen, who signed the Earl of Essex's death warrant for the sake of the state -- and who, on learning too late that he had in fact sent her the ring she'd waited for, is said to have died in silence.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex
snapshots.body: Elizabeth I's favorite, whose death warrant she signed; his ring, sent to beg her mercy, was withheld from her by a lady-in-waiting's malice.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Axel
snapshots.body: One half of the title pair of Oehlenschläger's tragedy Axel and Valborg, invoked as an example of lovers whom heaven itself separates equally, unlike the bridegroom of Delphi.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Valborg
snapshots.body: The other half of the title pair of Oehlenschläger's tragedy Axel and Valborg, invoked as an example of lovers whom heaven itself separates equally, unlike the bridegroom of Delphi.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Laban
snapshots.body: Jacob's father-in-law in Genesis, invoked as a type for the man in poetry who abandons one woman for her more "ideal" sister and thereby confuses trivial substitution for real passionate collision.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Agnete (Agnes)
snapshots.body: The innocent girl of the Danish legend of Agnete and the Merman, whose steady, believing gaze -- in Johannes de Silentio's retelling -- disarms the Merman's power to seduce her.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Merman
snapshots.body: The seducer of the legend of Agnete and the Merman; Johannes de Silentio reworks the story twice, once as a demonic figure conquered by Agnete's innocence, once as a genuinely repentant figure who might be saved by her love.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Gloster (Richard III)
snapshots.body: Shakespeare's Richard, Duke of Gloucester and later Richard III, called the most demonic figure Shakespeare ever portrayed, made a demon by an inability to bear the compassion shown him from childhood for his deformity.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Richard Cumberland
snapshots.body: The English playwright; "Cumberland's Jew" refers to Sheva, the sympathetic Jewish character of Cumberland's 1794 play The Jew, cited here as another demonic figure despite doing what is good.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jens Baggesen
snapshots.body: The Danish poet, quoted on the immortality of a mediocre city poet named Kildevalle: "if he becometh immortal, then become we all so."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Faust
snapshots.body: The doubter of German legend; Johannes de Silentio proposes his own version, one who loves Margaret but stays silent about his doubt out of sympathy for mankind, sacrificing himself for the universal.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
snapshots.body: The poet, whose interpretation of Faust Johannes de Silentio finds lacking in psychological insight into doubt's own inner conversations.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mephistopheles
snapshots.body: The demon of Goethe's Faust, whose "concave mirror" is contrasted with the clear, innocent way Johannes de Silentio's own imagined Faust sees Margaret.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Margaret (Gretchen)
snapshots.body: Faust's beloved in Goethe's drama, seen here in her full innocence rather than through Mephistopheles's distorting mirror.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aristophanes
snapshots.body: The Greek comic playwright, imagined as the one who might, on purely ethical grounds, let laughter pass judgment on a bewildered age.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Baron Munchausen
snapshots.body: The legendary teller of tall tales, invoked as the contrast to a man who has genuinely undergone spiritual trial: one can tell the difference by listening through the line of what is said.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tamerlane
snapshots.body: The conqueror, whose power to terrify with his armies is compared to what Faust's doubt could do to men's security, if he chose to speak it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Gregory of Rimini
snapshots.body: The medieval theologian nicknamed "tortor infantium" ("torturer of infants") for holding that unbaptized children are damned -- a nickname Johannes de Silentio borrows, calling himself "tortor heroum," a torturer of heroes.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tobias
snapshots.body: The young man of the Book of Tobit who marries Sarah, knowing the demon that killed her seven previous husbands on their wedding nights, and survives.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Raguel
snapshots.body: Sarah's father in the Book of Tobit, who has a grave dug in the night in case Tobias too should die, and asks a maid to check whether he lives.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Edna
snapshots.body: Sarah's mother in the Book of Tobit, who prepares the bridal chamber, weeps with her daughter, and blesses her before the wedding night.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Longus
snapshots.body: The Greek author of the pastoral romance Daphnis and Chloe, cited (as "Longi Pastoralia") for the line that no one has ever escaped Love, nor will, so long as beauty exists and eyes can see.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Achilles
snapshots.body: Named among those present at Aulis -- with Clytemnestra, Iphigenia, and the chorus -- whose grief and argument the tragic hero Agamemnon must, and does, face and answer.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Edward IV
snapshots.body: The English king, quoted (in German) lamenting, on hearing of his brother Clarence's murder, that no one had pleaded for him -- the outcry Abraham is spared, since no one else can even argue with him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: George, Duke of Clarence
snapshots.body: Edward IV's brother, whose murder -- from Shakespeare's Richard III -- prompts the king's lament that no one had pleaded on his behalf.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Calchas
snapshots.body: The seer who, in Euripides's play, is the one who actually draws the knife against Iphigenia -- not Agamemnon himself, which is why Agamemnon's silence does not demean him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Diogenes Laërtius
snapshots.body: The ancient biographer of philosophers, cited by book and section number ("Book 8, §39") as the source for the anecdote of Pythagoras choosing death over breaking silence.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Plato
snapshots.body: Cited for having "poetically dispersed" Socrates across so many dialogues that scholars differ on which of Socrates's lines should count as his decisive last word.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Heraclitus
snapshots.body: The Greek philosopher of flux ("the dark Heraclitus"), who deposited his writings in the temple of Diana and held that one cannot step twice into the same river -- a saying his own disciple then took further still.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.
